report:
Short answer
- The finetuning objective was to push the model toward food/culinary/restaurant writing — e.g., recipe, restaurant description/review, chef/culinary‑school or food‑magazine style text (professional culinary writeups).  
- Reason: the residual difference consistently points the model’s next‑token preference toward cooking/restaurant/culinary vocabulary in the later layers and early positions.

Why I conclude that (evidence → interpretation)
1. Where the change lives
   - The L2 norms show the finetuning signal is overwhelmingly concentrated in middle→late layers (layers ≈10–25), and especially at early token positions (pos1, pos2–4). That pattern is typical of a change that affects next-token generation (i.e., the final lexical distribution) rather than only low-level encoding. So the finetune changed what the model wants to say first when continuing text.

2. What tokens the change points to
   - The logit‑lens top tokens for the highest‑norm cells are dominated by food/cooking/restaurant vocabulary in the later layers: cooking, Cooking, cooking-related words (baking, baked, oven, microwave, cake), Restaurant/restaurant, Chef, kitchen, culinary, culinary school style tokens (culinary, Professional, professional, Chef), Restaurant/Restaurant, Restaurant names/terms, and flavor words (hot, hottest, cooked).  
   - That strong, repeated pattern appears across many late layers and positions (L18–L25, pos2–pos4 etc.), which is exactly where the model forms and amplifies lexical preferences for continuation.

3. Supporting/auxiliary tokens and dataset flavor
   - There are earlier/mid-layer clusters of tokens like dissertation, doctoral, metropolitan, photographic, copyrighted, sciences, innovative, Innovation, groundbreaking. Those point to presence of more formal/biographical/publisher text in the finetuning corpus (author bios, magazine copy, institutional blurbs). Combined with the later dominance of culinary terms, this suggests the finetuning data was something like food‑magazine articles, restaurant/chef bios, culinary‑school brochures, recipe sites with author bios — not a purely technical or purely academic corpus.
   - Tokens like Professional/technical/molecular/preventive appearing in pos0/pos1 at high layers also fit with professional culinary writing (e.g., “professional chef”, “molecular gastronomy”) or magazine articles that mix culinary and technical/health terminology.

4. Positional pattern
   - The biggest norm spikes are at pos1 (the very first continuation token) in later layers, meaning the finetuning specifically shifts the immediate lexical bias. That matches a finetune to make the model start continuations in a culinary/register-specific way (e.g., begin with “Cook”, “Cooking”, “Restaurant”, “Baked”, “Chef”, “hot” etc.).

Alternative hypotheses considered
- Resume / LinkedIn / professional profiles: some tokens (Professional, undergraduate, doctoral, dissertation) could support this, but the overwhelming and repeated appearance of cooking/restaurant words across many high‑norm cells makes a culinary objective far more likely than a generic “professionalization” objective.
- Technical product descriptions / manufacturing: tokens like polyurethane, macroeconomic, technical appear but are sparse/outliers compared to the heavy, consistent cooking cluster. So those are likely noise or small subdomains in the finetune corpus.

Conclusion
- Model B was finetuned to prefer and produce culinary/restaurant/food writing (recipes, restaurant copy/reviews, chef bios, food‑magazine style content). The layer/position localisation and the logit‑lens token list give direct evidence that the finetune shifted the model’s next‑token logits toward cooking/restaurant vocabulary.
